Road days come off the spring and fall limits as your coaches travel, and your budget decides who flies.
Calls to busy high school coaches leave a message, and they call back in their planning period; your men phone in from the road at night.

Word gets around: what you do for one coach's kid reaches his staff and his area.

Offer a kid the world rates low and he becomes your find. Every step he climbs lifts the coach who told you and your name as a finder.

Ask a coach for his read on a player and he tells you where that player stands at his spot, how high he could go, and whether he'd keep him.

bullets: A new Ground screen, The meeting, with the road days and your free hours for the week.
Each place that wants a man is a numbered stop on the map, with who goes and where you stand there.

Receivers, backs and defensive backs vary in height and weight like real players.

High school coaches fill their rosters closer to real position shares.

The very fastest 3-cones and shuttles are rare, as they are in real life.

A young coach can ride along with a veteran and meet his high school coaches.
When another school wants one of your men, you get a few days to counter with a raise, a title or a promise.
A coach who leaves takes his ties with him, and the kids he recruited may waver until you call them.
As an assistant, bring your head coach two kids a week; he signs them or says wait, and his August verdict follows you.

Every Monday you can change your own goal, and your coordinator warns you when one slips.
Long shots pay the most when you make them; sure things cost the most when you miss.
In your first offseason your coordinator walks you through your ground, three schools at a time, until you send him off.

Junior days, visit weekends and the spring game let you sit with families, hear from player hosts and offer on the spot; from 2027 the spring game is yours to hold or skip.

Other staffs find kids through the people they know, not by magic.

Your starters stay off kickoff coverage. Backups cover kicks, so your best edge no longer pads his tackles there.
A player who came over from another sport can now be moved to the position his body fits, so no more 167-pound defensive tackles piling up sacks.
Record books in a world you already play keep their old numbers; games from here on use the new counts.

bullets: Collectives now pay each player up to his market price on top of what the school shares with him, instead of splitting their money by a separate formula.
Pay follows today's depth chart, so a player who wins a starting job is paid like a starter that summer.
The best-paid quarterbacks come down to what real stars make, and starters at the other positions come up.
The going rate on your NIL desk reads the same market, so it matches what rival schools pay.

bullets: An owner now gives a new head coach real time: a bad first month in your first season is not a firing matter.
When your job is in doubt you hear it from the owner, and the news carries it. He can only make a change from the Monday after.
If the team steadies, the talk dies down and you are told so.
An owner who nearly fired you after the season says so: you start the next one on the hot seat.
Every other club's coach is on the same rules, so in-season firings around the league come at real times too.

657.title: NFL head coaches: a public hot seat before any in-season firing
657.tldr: Your NFL owner no longer fires you out of the blue. If your seat gets hot he tells you first, and you get at least a week to turn it around.

bullets: A returning redshirt or young backup who has earned a place is paid by his school, even with no deal.
The lowest-paid players on a major roster get a real stipend again, not a token one.
Schools stop making keep-him offers to walk-ons and deep backups they would not pay anyway.
The very top quarterback checks come down into the real range.
658.look: your NIL desk's roster split in a second season, and what your backups and redshirts are paid in July.
658.title: NIL deals in later years: the paid set by standing, a deal's school part by standing, keep-him offers only to men a school pays
658.tldr: College pay stays realistic after the first year. Schools now pay players by where they stand on the team, not by who happened to hold a deal first.

bullets: Linebackers, corners and safeties who blitz creep up before the snap and get to the passer as often as real blitzers do.
Offensive lines pick up the rush man for man across the formation, so an edge rusher no longer runs free because a guard was sent out to him.
Quarterbacks throw hot right away when a blitzer they know is free is coming, and backs check for the blitz at the snap.
A pass rusher's pressures now count every hurry, hit and sack, and his rushes count once a play.

659.tldr: Blitzes now get home like real ones, and pass protection blocks the way real lines are taught.

bullets: A coordinator compares his backs, receivers and passers with the rest of his own league, not with a fixed yardstick, before he leans his calls toward them.
College offenses run outside about a sixth less often, and run games and deep throws land closer to real numbers.
Defenses weigh their linebackers, corners and safeties against their own league when they pick blitzes and coverages.
Saved games and replays keep the same reads.

660.tldr: Play callers now judge their players against the players in their own league, so college offenses stop running wide and throwing deep on every down.

Weak quarterback classes still let a great edge rusher or corner go first.

bullets: Tackles take a vertical set against a man rushing round the edge, and meet him two yards behind the line.
An end who beats his man now does it close to the quarterback, so it shows up as pressure.
The spare lineman in a four-man rush helps the block that is losing, not just the one nearest him.
Inside tackles no longer get a free single block on every snap, so edges out-sack them as in the real game.

663.title: The four-man rush: the tackle's vertical set and the spare man's eyes (realism audit item 3)
663.tldr: Edge rushers play like edge rushers now: tackles kick back to meet them behind the line, so an end who wins is on the quarterback. Watch the best ends' pressures and sacks climb, while the spare lineman helps where the trouble is.

bullets: Each point of recruiting skill builds a recruit's bond with a coach faster than before.
A typical head coach recruits as he did; strong recruiters pull clear and weak ones fall behind.
Programs rise and fall more with who coaches them, so eras come and go over ten years.
Transfers weigh a strong recruiter's calls more too.

664.title: Program fortunes measuring pass: size the recruiting bond's curve on four seeds
664.tldr: A great recruiter now changes a program. Your head coach's and position coaches' recruiting ratings decide far more of the close battles for a recruit.

bullets: Defenses match one, two, three and four receivers with four, five or six backs as real NFL defenses do on each down.
Every defensive coordinator has his own nickel and dime habits, so some staffs live in dime on third and long and others almost never play it.
A team's third safety now plays as the big nickel or the dime back when he is the better man for the job.
A defender who forces a runner out of bounds gets the tackle in the box score.
Kickers rarely make the tackle on a kickoff now, and punt teams line up like real ones.

665.title: Who is on the field and who gets the tackle: the real table of backs, the third safety, the sideline credit (realism audit item 3)
665.tldr: Defenses now put the right men on the field. They answer your receivers with nickel and dime packages as often as real staffs do, and a third safety can be the extra back when he fits the job better than a corner.

bullets: A shared tackle in the pros can now be a tackle with an assist: the man who made it keeps his solo tackle and the man beside him gets the assist.
Linemen and linebackers in on short runs get the credit real scorers give them.
A shared tackle for loss goes whole to the man who made it.
Film and scouting reports still praise only the man who made the tackle.

bullets: From 2027 the salary cap is set from league revenue each year, one cap for every club.
The cap no longer runs away from what clubs earn, so player pay stays about the real share of revenue.
Contracts, rookie deals, tags and the minimum all move with the new cap.

A linebacker who misreads the run fills the wrong gap and stays there, so a back with vision can find the hole he left.
The running game keeps its real yards a carry in the NFL and college.

bullets: College staffs of every system call their quarterback's runs, more of them the quicker he is against the men in his league.

A quarterback who keeps it now runs at full speed around the end instead of jogging behind his back.
